swat-streaming is a small, containerized bridge that consumes a Kafka topic and writes the messages into a SAS Viya CAS in-memory table using the SWAT Python client. It is built for deployments where SAS Viya cannot subscribe to Kafka natively and you want streaming data available in CAS for downstream analytics: dashboards in SAS Visual Analytics, model scoring, or ad-hoc exploration in SAS Studio.

Batching. Messages are written to CAS in batches, triggered by size (BATCH_SIZE) or time (BATCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), so you don't pay CAS's per-call overhead for every message. At-least-once delivery. Kafka offsets are committed only after the batch has landed in CAS. A crash replays the batch; no message is silently lost. Kafka lineage on every row. Each row gets _kafka_topic, _kafka_partition, _kafka_offset, _kafka_timestamp and _ingested_at columns, which you can use for deduplication and auditing. Secure by default. SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 over TLS for Kafka, OAuth bearer tokens for CAS, credentials read from mounted files instead of environment variables, and a non-root, read-only container. Horizontal scaling. Replicas share a Kafka consumer group, and partitions are rebalanced across pods automatically. Built-in load generator. A synthetic card-transaction producer with labeled fraud patterns ships in the same image, so you can test the pipeline end to end.

Path Purpose app/ The consumer: Kafka source, message parser, CAS writer, and the batching loop producer/ Synthetic Kafka producer (card-fraud transactions) for end-to-end testing Dockerfile Slim, non-root image that contains both the consumer and the producer requirements.txt Pinned Python dependencies k8s/ Namespace, ConfigMap, Deployment, NetworkPolicy, producer Job, example Secret, Kustomization website/ This documentation site

The consumer is a single-threaded loop with four building blocks: Module Responsibility app/kafka_consumer.py (KafkaSource) Subscribes to the topic, polls batches, and commits offsets explicitly app/message_parser.py Decodes each payload (json or raw) and adds Kafka metadata columns app/cas_writer.py (CASWriter) Opens the CAS session and loads batches into the target table app/main.py (StreamRunner) Wires everything together, runs the loop, and handles shutdown signals All configuration comes from environment variables (app/config.py). See the configuration reference.

Each iteration: Poll. Asks Kafka for up to BATCH_SIZE messages and waits at most BATCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS. If nothing arrives, the loop polls again. Partition-EOF events are ignored; any other Kafka error stops the process. Parse. Decodes every message according to MESSAGE_FORMAT: json: the payload must be a UTF-8 JSON object. Each top-level key becomes a column. raw: the payload is decoded as UTF-8 (invalid bytes are replaced) into a single value column. Messages that can't be parsed are logged as Skipping unparseable message and skipped, but their offsets are still committed. There is no dead-letter queue. Enrich. Adds lineage columns to each record. If the payload already has a field with the same name, the payload value wins. Column Content _kafka_topic Source topic _kafka_partition Source partition _kafka_offset Offset within the partition _kafka_timestamp Kafka message timestamp (epoch milliseconds) _ingested_at UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of when the consumer processed the message Write. Builds a pandas DataFrame from the batch and loads it into CAS (see below). Commit. Commits the highest offset per partition, synchronously, only after the write succeeded.

First batch. If the target table didn't exist when the CAS session was opened, the first batch creates it with upload_frame. When CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE=true, the table is promoted to global scope, so other CAS sessions (SAS Studio, Visual Analytics, and so on) can see it. Later batches. Each batch is uploaded to a uniquely named staging table and appended to the target with table.append. The staging table is then dropped, even if the append failed. Staging names include the process ID and a random suffix, so several replicas never collide. Column types are fixed by the first batch. upload_frame infers CAS column types from the DataFrame. Later batches must stay compatible with that schema. See schema changes. Retries. write_batch is retried on SWATError up to 5 times with exponential backoff (1 s to 30 s). If every attempt fails, the error propagates, the process exits with code 1, and Kubernetes restarts the pod. Because the offsets were never committed, the batch is replayed.

swat-streaming provides at-least-once delivery: A message's offset is committed only after its batch is in CAS, so a crash never loses data. A crash after the CAS write but before the commit replays the whole batch on restart, which creates duplicate rows. Use _kafka_topic + _kafka_partition + _kafka_offset as a natural key to deduplicate downstream. Make sure consumers of the CAS table either tolerate duplicates or deduplicate on that key.

Configuration is loaded and validated. A missing required variable exits immediately with code 2. The Kafka consumer subscribes and the CAS session connects. The writer records whether the target table already exists. The loop runs until SIGTERM or SIGINT. In the container, tini is PID 1 and forwards signals to Python. On shutdown, the current batch finishes, and then the Kafka consumer and CAS session are closed. If CAS_PERSIST_ON_SHUTDOWN=true, the in-memory table is saved to the caslib first (as <table>.<CAS_PERSIST_FORMAT>). Exit code Meaning 0 Clean shutdown after a signal 1 Fatal runtime error (Kafka error, CAS write failed after retries, and so on) 2 Configuration error (required environment variable missing)

Every log line is a single JSON object on stdout, with ts, level, logger and message fields plus structured context: {"ts": "2026-05-27 10:42:13,812", "level": "INFO", "logger": "app.main", "message": "Batch processed", "received": 500, "written": 498, "parse_failures": 2} The kafka and swat library loggers are capped at WARNING. Credentials are never logged. The CAS connection line only says "auth": "token" or "auth": "password".

Streaming from Kafka into CAS crosses two trust boundaries, and each one needs its own credentials. Neither set should ever end up in a container image, a Git repository, or shell history. Hop Recommended Configured with Kafka SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512 over TLS kafka-credentials Secret (username, password, CA) CAS OAuth bearer token from SAS Logon Manager cas-credentials Secret (token, CA bundle) mTLS for Kafka and username/password for CAS are also supported.

This is the app's default. It gives you: transport encryption (TLS 1.2+) a password that is never sent over the wire (SCRAM uses challenge/response) per-user credentials that you can revoke without restarting brokers On the Kafka cluster (one-time, by your Kafka administrator): # Create a SCRAM user kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9093 \ --alter --add-config 'SCRAM-SHA-512=[password=REPLACE_ME]' \ --entity-type users --entity-name svc-viya-consumer # Grant read on the topic and the consumer group kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9093 \ --add --allow-principal User:svc-viya-consumer \ --operation Read --operation Describe \ --topic viya.events --group swat-streaming-viya-events In the pod, provide the credentials through the mounted kafka-credentials Secret: Mount path Secret key Used as /etc/kafka/credentials/username username SASL username (KAFKA_SASL_USERNAME_FILE) /etc/kafka/credentials/password password SASL password (KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD_FILE) /etc/kafka/certs/ca.crt ca.crt Trust anchor for the broker certificate (KAFKA_SSL_CA_LOCATION)

If your Kafka cluster authenticates clients by certificate, set KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL=SSL and mount: Variable File mounted from a Secret KAFKA_SSL_CA_LOCATION /etc/kafka/certs/ca.crt KAFKA_SSL_CERTIFICATE_LOCATION /etc/kafka/certs/client.crt KAFKA_SSL_KEY_LOCATION /etc/kafka/certs/client.key Remove the SASL username/password mount. The principal is the subject of the client certificate, so grant ACLs against that DN. mTLS is operationally harder than SCRAM (certificate rotation, CRL management), but it's the better fit in environments that already standardize on PKI.

The synthetic producer needs different permissions than the consumer. Provision a separate Kafka principal and Secret for it rather than reusing the consumer's: # On the Kafka cluster: producer-only ACL kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9093 \ --add --allow-principal User:svc-viya-producer \ --operation Write --operation Describe \ --topic viya.events # In the cluster: a separate Secret kubectl -n swat-streaming create secret generic kafka-producer-credentials \ --from-literal=username='svc-viya-producer' \ --from-literal=password='REPLACE_ME' \ --from-file=ca.crt=./kafka-ca.crt Then point the volumes in k8s/producer-job.yaml at kafka-producer-credentials instead of kafka-credentials. With split principals, the consumer stays read-only: a compromised consumer pod can't inject messages, and a compromised producer pod can't read messages or commit offsets.
SASL_PLAINTEXT sends credentials over the network unencrypted. PLAINTEXT has no authentication and no encryption. Use it only in a lab. SASL/PLAIN over TLS works, but SCRAM is strictly better.
The container talks to CAS through SWAT's HTTPS (REST) protocol. These are the options, in order of preference.

SAS Logon Manager issues OAuth2 access tokens, each bound to a registered client and usually to a service user. SWAT accepts the token as its password argument over HTTPS. One-time setup (Viya administrator). Register a client that can obtain tokens for the service user, for example with sas-admin: sas-admin auth login sas-admin oauthclient create \ --client-id swat-streaming \ --client-secret 'REPLACE_ME' \ --scope 'openid' \ --grant-type password \ --access-token-validity 43200 \ --refresh-token-validity 2592000 Grant the client only the scopes it needs. Don't give the streaming client administrative scopes. Get a token. Do this outside the cluster, for example in CI or your secret manager, and store the resulting access_token in the cas-credentials Secret under the key token: ACCESS_TOKEN=$(curl -sS -u "swat-streaming:REPLACE_ME" \ -d 'grant_type=password' \ -d 'username=svc-viya-streamer' \ -d 'password=REPLACE_ME' \ https://viya.example.com/SASLogon/oauth/token | jq -r .access_token) The app reads the token from CAS_TOKEN_FILE=/etc/cas/credentials/token. Token expiry Viya access tokens are short-lived (12 hours by default), and the app reads the token only once, at startup. For long-running pods, use one of these: a sidecar that refreshes the token with the refresh token and writes it to a shared volume, combined with periodic pod restarts External Secrets Operator with a generator that calls SAS Logon, plus a rollout when the Secret changes a Vault Agent template that writes a fresh token to disk If none of these are available, set the access-token validity long enough to cover the pod's lifetime and rotate with a scheduled redeploy.
documents.s: Recommended: OAuth token from SAS Logon Manager

documents.t: If OAuth isn't available, set CAS_USERNAME_FILE and CAS_PASSWORD_FILE instead of CAS_TOKEN_FILE. Always use a dedicated service user from your identity provider, never a personal account.

Kerberos is possible but heavy to operate in containers (keytab management, clock skew, KDC reachability). If you must use it, mount the keytab from a Secret, install krb5-user in the image, and provide /etc/krb5.conf through a ConfigMap. Treat it as a last resort.

Authentication only proves who the caller is. The service user still needs authorization in CAS. On the target caslib, grant: ReadInfo, Select, CreateTable, LimitedPromote, and Promote (only if CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE=true) Grant nothing more. The service user shouldn't have administrative privileges. In SAS Environment Manager, these settings are under Data → Libraries → (your caslib) → Authorization.

Whichever tool you use, the contract with the app is the same: credentials show up as files under /etc/kafka/credentials/ and /etc/cas/credentials/, the *_FILE environment variables point at those files, and the app reads them at startup. Plain environment-variable secrets also work but are discouraged, because they appear in kubectl describe pod output.

Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded at rest by default. Before relying on them, check that: etcd encryption at rest is enabled, with a KMS provider RBAC limits get / list on Secrets in the swat-streaming namespace to a small set of principals audit logging records Secret reads

Tool Why External Secrets Operator Syncs secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, or Vault into Kubernetes Secrets. Your enterprise secret store stays the source of truth. Sealed Secrets Encrypts Secret manifests with a key that only the cluster can decrypt, so the sealed manifests are safe to commit to Git. Vault Agent Injector Writes secrets straight into the pod as files, without ever creating a Secret object. Secrets Store CSI Driver Mounts secrets from an external store as files through CSI, with native rotation support.

The app doesn't re-read credentials while it runs. After rotating any credential, update the Secret and then restart the Deployment: kubectl -n swat-streaming rollout restart deploy/swat-streaming Credential Procedure Kafka SCRAM password Change it on the broker → update the Secret → restart Kafka CA Roll out the new CA in the Secret → restart CAS OAuth token Automated refresh (see token expiry) → restart CAS password Rotate in the identity provider → update the Secret → restart

etcd encryption at rest is enabled with a KMS provider. The NetworkPolicy (k8s/networkpolicy.yaml) allows egress only to the Kafka brokers and the Viya CAS endpoint, with the CIDRs narrowed to your networks. The pod runs as non-root (runAsNonRoot: true, UID 10001). The pod has readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and drops all capabilities. Secrets are mounted as files with mode 0400, not passed as environment variables. automountServiceAccountToken: false is set. The app never calls the Kubernetes API. The Kafka consumer principal has read-only ACLs on exactly one topic. If you run the synthetic producer, it uses a separate principal with only Write + Describe on the topic. The CAS service user has the minimum caslib permissions for the target table. OAuth tokens are short-lived and rotated automatically. The image is signed (for example with cosign) and pinned by digest in the Deployment. Logs contain no credentials. The app only logs auth: token or auth: password, never the value.

All configuration comes from environment variables. In Kubernetes, non-sensitive values come from the swat-streaming-config ConfigMap, and credentials come from files mounted from Secrets. File-based secrets Every credential has a *_FILE variant. When X_FILE is set, the app reads the value from that file (with surrounding whitespace stripped) and ignores the plain X variable. File-based secrets are recommended because, unlike environment variables, they don't show up in kubectl describe pod or in process listings. Boolean variables are true only when their value is the string true (case-insensitive). Any other value counts as false.

Variable Default Description KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS required Comma-separated host:port broker list KAFKA_TOPIC required Topic to consume (or, for the producer, to produce to) KAFKA_GROUP_ID required Consumer group ID. Also required by the producer, which ignores it KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL SASL_SSL SASL_SSL, SSL, SASL_PLAINTEXT, or PLAINTEXT KAFKA_SASL_MECHANISM SCRAM-SHA-512 SCRAM-SHA-512, SCRAM-SHA-256, or PLAIN. Used only with SASL_* protocols KAFKA_SASL_USERNAME / KAFKA_SASL_USERNAME_FILE – SASL username KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD / KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD_FILE – SASL password KAFKA_SSL_CA_LOCATION – Path to the CA certificate that signed the broker certificates. Used with SSL / SASL_SSL KAFKA_SSL_CERTIFICATE_LOCATION – Client certificate path, for mTLS KAFKA_SSL_KEY_LOCATION – Client private key path, for mTLS KAFKA_AUTO_OFFSET_RESET latest Where a new consumer group starts: latest or earliest KAFKA_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MS 45000 Consumer group session timeout KAFKA_MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS 300000 Maximum time between polls before the consumer is evicted from the group. Must be longer than your slowest CAS write, including retries Auto-commit is always disabled. Offsets are committed by the app after each successful CAS write.

Variable Default Description CAS_HOST required For https: the full URL of the CAS REST endpoint, for example https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http. For cas: the controller hostname CAS_PORT – CAS port. Usually unset for REST URLs; for example 5570 for the binary protocol CAS_PROTOCOL https https / http (REST) or cas (binary) CAS_TOKEN / CAS_TOKEN_FILE – OAuth access token. When set, it is used instead of username/password CAS_USERNAME / CAS_USERNAME_FILE – CAS username (used only when no token is set) CAS_PASSWORD / CAS_PASSWORD_FILE – CAS password (used only when no token is set) CAS_SSL_CA_LIST – Path to the CA bundle used to verify the Viya TLS certificate CAS_CASLIB CASUSER Caslib that holds the target table. Must already exist CAS_TABLE_NAME kafka_stream Name of the in-memory target table CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE true Promote the table to global scope when it is created, so other sessions can read it CAS_PERSIST_ON_SHUTDOWN false On graceful shutdown, save the table to the caslib's data source CAS_PERSIST_FORMAT parquet File extension and format used when persisting, for example parquet or sashdat

Variable Default Description BATCH_SIZE 500 Maximum messages per poll, and therefore per CAS write BATCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 5 Maximum time to wait while filling a batch MESSAGE_FORMAT json json (each payload must be a JSON object) or raw (payload stored as text in a value column) LOG_LEVEL INFO Python log level: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR

The producer (python -m producer.main) reads all the KAFKA_* variables above for connectivity, plus these: Variable Default Description PRODUCER_RATE_PER_SECOND 50 Target send rate (best effort, evenly paced) PRODUCER_DURATION_SECONDS unset Stop after N seconds PRODUCER_TOTAL_MESSAGES unset Stop after N messages PRODUCER_NUM_ACCOUNTS 5000 Size of the card/account pool PRODUCER_NUM_MERCHANTS 800 Size of the merchant pool PRODUCER_FRAUD_RATE 0.01 Probability that a given emission starts a fraud burst PRODUCER_SEED unset Seed for the random generator, for reproducible runs PRODUCER_FLUSH_EVERY 500 Log a progress line every N messages KAFKA_DEBUG unset librdkafka debug contexts, for example broker,security, for troubleshooting connections LOG_LEVEL INFO Python log level If neither PRODUCER_DURATION_SECONDS nor PRODUCER_TOTAL_MESSAGES is set, the producer runs until it gets SIGTERM / SIGINT. The producer's Kafka client is configured with acks=all, idempotence enabled, and zstd compression.

apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: swat-streaming-config namespace: swat-streaming data: KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: "kafka-broker-1.example.com:9093,kafka-broker-2.example.com:9093" KAFKA_TOPIC: "viya.events" KAFKA_GROUP_ID: "swat-streaming-viya-events" KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL: "SASL_SSL" KAFKA_SASL_MECHANISM: "SCRAM-SHA-512" KAFKA_SSL_CA_LOCATION: "/etc/kafka/certs/ca.crt" KAFKA_AUTO_OFFSET_RESET: "latest" CAS_HOST: "https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http" CAS_PROTOCOL: "https" CAS_CASLIB: "Public" CAS_TABLE_NAME: "kafka_stream" CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE: "true" CAS_SSL_CA_LIST: "/etc/cas/certs/ca-bundle.crt" CAS_PERSIST_ON_SHUTDOWN: "false" BATCH_SIZE: "500" BATCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "5" MESSAGE_FORMAT: "json" LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
This guide walks through building the container image and deploying the swat-streaming workload into a Kubernetes cluster that can reach both your Kafka brokers and the SAS Viya CAS endpoint.

Requirement Notes Kafka cluster Reachable from the cluster; TLS strongly recommended Kafka topic Pre-created; the partition count sets the maximum parallelism Kafka service account (consumer) Read access to the topic, member of the consumer group Kafka service account (producer, optional) Write + Describe ACL on the topic. Only needed for the synthetic producer SAS Viya Reachable HTTPS endpoint of the CAS server, for example https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http Viya service user SAS user with permission on the target caslib (see CAS authorization) OAuth client (optional, recommended) Registered in SAS Logon Manager to issue access tokens Kubernetes 1.24+ With a working kubectl / kustomize workflow Container registry To host the built image

From the repository root: docker build -t ghcr.io/your-org/swat-streaming:0.1.0 . docker push ghcr.io/your-org/swat-streaming:0.1.0 What the image contains: Python 3.11 slim base, running as UID/GID 10001:10001 tini as PID 1, so signals are forwarded cleanly librdkafka1, used by confluent-kafka libnuma1 and libgomp1. The SWAT wheel bundles SAS TK shared libraries and loads them at import time, even when only the REST protocol is used. Without libnuma1, import swat fails with Cannot dlopen [tkmk.so] : [libnuma.so.1: cannot open shared object file]. Both entrypoints: python -m app.main (the default, the consumer) and python -m producer.main (the test producer) REST vs. binary protocol By default the container talks to CAS over HTTPS with SWAT's REST protocol. This is the recommended setup for streaming because it passes through ingress controllers and firewalls cleanly and authenticates with OAuth. To use the CAS binary protocol (port 5570) instead, set CAS_PROTOCOL=cas and point CAS_HOST / CAS_PORT at the CAS controller. No image changes are needed. Update image: in k8s/deployment.yaml (and k8s/producer-job.yaml) to match the tag you pushed. For production, pin the image by digest.

Non-sensitive settings live in the swat-streaming-config ConfigMap (k8s/configmap.yaml). Credentials and TLS material live in Secrets. At minimum, edit: Variable Purpose KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS Comma-separated host:port list KAFKA_TOPIC Topic to subscribe to KAFKA_GROUP_ID Consumer group; controls offset tracking CAS_HOST Full URL of the CAS HTTP endpoint CAS_CASLIB Target caslib (must already exist, for example Public) CAS_TABLE_NAME In-memory CAS table that receives the stream The configuration reference lists every supported variable. Tuning batches CAS appends have noticeable per-call overhead, so prefer larger batches (500–5000 rows) over small ones. Combine BATCH_SIZE with BATCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS so that batches still flush regularly when traffic is low. Also adjust k8s/networkpolicy.yaml. The shipped policy allows egress to 10.0.0.0/8 on ports 9093 (Kafka), 443 and 8777 (CAS REST), plus DNS. Narrow the CIDRs to your actual broker and Viya networks, and change the ports if yours differ. kubectl apply -f k8s/namespace.yaml kubectl apply -f k8s/configmap.yaml

The Deployment expects two Secrets in the swat-streaming namespace: Secret Keys Mounted at kafka-credentials username, password, ca.crt /etc/kafka/credentials/, /etc/kafka/certs/ cas-credentials token (or username + password), ca-bundle.crt /etc/cas/credentials/, /etc/cas/certs/ For a controlled lab environment: kubectl -n swat-streaming create secret generic kafka-credentials \ --from-literal=username='svc-viya-consumer' \ --from-literal=password='REPLACE_ME' \ --from-file=ca.crt=./kafka-ca.crt kubectl -n swat-streaming create secret generic cas-credentials \ --from-literal=token='REPLACE_ME_OAUTH_TOKEN' \ --from-file=ca-bundle.crt=./viya-ca-bundle.crt warning k8s/secret.example.yaml is intentionally not part of the Kustomization. Never commit real Secret manifests. For production, use External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets, or Vault Agent Injector. See Authentication. If you authenticate to CAS with username/password instead of a token, edit k8s/deployment.yaml: remove CAS_TOKEN_FILE, add CAS_USERNAME_FILE and CAS_PASSWORD_FILE, and adjust the cas-creds volume items to match.

kubectl apply -k k8s/ kubectl -n swat-streaming rollout status deploy/swat-streaming kubectl -n swat-streaming logs -f deploy/swat-streaming A healthy consumer logs a startup line, then one line per batch: {"ts":"...","level":"INFO","logger":"app.main","message":"swat-streaming starting","topic":"viya.events","table":"Public.kafka_stream","batch_size":500} {"ts":"...","level":"INFO","logger":"app.cas_writer","message":"CAS session established","existing_target_table":false} {"ts":"...","level":"INFO","logger":"app.main","message":"Batch processed","received":500,"written":500,"parse_failures":0} The Deployment uses the Recreate strategy, a non-root security context with a read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, and automountServiceAccountToken: false.

If there is no live data on the topic yet, run the synthetic producer first. From SAS Studio, or any Python environment with SWAT: import swat conn = swat.CAS("https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http", username="...", password="...") conn.table.tableInfo(caslib="Public") conn.CASTable("kafka_stream", caslib="Public").head(20) With CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE=true, the table appears under the configured caslib for every Viya user with read permission on it.
Scale out, persist the table, and handle schema changes: Operations Harden credentials and plan rotation: Authentication

app/ main.py # StreamRunner: batch loop, signal handling, entrypoint config.py # Env-var configuration dataclasses (Kafka, CAS, stream) kafka_consumer.py # KafkaSource: poll batches, commit offsets message_parser.py # parse_message (json/raw) and enrich (Kafka metadata) cas_writer.py # CASWriter: connect, initial load, staged append, save logging_setup.py # JSON logging to stdout producer/ main.py # Producer loop: rate limiting, stop conditions, delivery callbacks config.py # PRODUCER_* settings and the Kafka producer configuration generator.py # TransactionGenerator: accounts, merchants, fraud bursts The producer reuses app.config.KafkaConfig and app.logging_setup, so changes there affect both entrypoints.

Requirements: Python 3.11, plus a Kafka broker and a CAS server you can reach. The container image is the reference environment. On Linux, the SWAT wheel also needs libnuma1 and libgomp1 (see Deployment). python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt For a throwaway single-node Kafka broker on localhost:9092, you can use the official Apache Kafka image: docker run -d --name kafka -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:3.8.0 Start the consumer against it: export KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS=localhost:9092 export KAFKA_TOPIC=viya.events export KAFKA_GROUP_ID=swat-streaming-dev export KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL=PLAINTEXT export KAFKA_AUTO_OFFSET_RESET=earliest export CAS_HOST=https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http export CAS_TOKEN_FILE=$HOME/.viya/token # or CAS_USERNAME / CAS_PASSWORD export CAS_CASLIB=CASUSER export CAS_TABLE_NAME=kafka_stream_dev export LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG python -m app.main In a second terminal, with the same KAFKA_* variables, generate traffic: PRODUCER_RATE_PER_SECOND=20 PRODUCER_TOTAL_MESSAGES=1000 PRODUCER_SEED=1 \ python -m producer.main Or run both from the image you built: docker build -t swat-streaming:dev . docker run --rm --network host --env-file dev.env swat-streaming:dev # consumer docker run --rm --network host --env-file dev.env swat-streaming:dev python -m producer.main # producer tip Leave dev.env and any token files out of version control. The repository's .dockerignore already excludes .env and .env.*.

Configuration goes through the dataclasses in app/config.py. Add new settings as fields with a from_env() mapping, use _file_or_env for anything secret, and document new variables in the configuration reference and k8s/configmap.yaml. Logging uses structured context: log.info("Message", extra={"key": value}), not string formatting. Never log credentials. Offset commits happen only after a successful CAS write. Keep that ordering whenever you change the loop in app/main.py. Dependencies are pinned exactly in requirements.txt. Source file headers. The documentation site is built with Docusaurus from the website/ directory. The pages are Markdown (MDX) files in website/docs/, and the sidebar order comes from each page's sidebar_position front matter. cd website npm ci npm start # live-reloading dev server at http://localhost:3000/swat-streaming/ npm run build # production build into website/build (fails on broken links) On every push to main, the Deploy Doc Website to GitHub Pages workflow builds the site and publishes it to GitHub Pages. Diagrams are written in Mermaid inside a fenced mermaid code block.

Maintainers accept patches and contributions to this project. Please read the contribution guidelines and the SAS Open Source Contributor Handbook. Contributions must follow the Contributor Agreement. External contributors must sign off their commits (git commit -s). The DCO check enforces this on pull requests. All submissions, including those from project members, are reviewed through GitHub pull requests.

Vertical. Increase BATCH_SIZE and the pod's memory limit. CAS usually becomes the bottleneck before Kafka does, and larger batches spread the per-call overhead over more rows. The default resources are 200m CPU / 512Mi requested and 1 CPU / 1Gi limit. Horizontal. Increase replicas in k8s/deployment.yaml, up to the topic's partition count. All pods join the same KAFKA_GROUP_ID, and Kafka spreads partitions across them. Pods beyond the partition count sit idle. Multiple topics. Deploy one instance per topic, each with its own ConfigMap, consumer group, and target table. Creating the table with several replicas A replica that doesn't find the target table at startup creates it with replace=True on its first batch. If several replicas start before the table exists, they can each create the table and overwrite each other's first batch. Start with a single replica until the table exists, then scale up.

A promoted CAS table lives in memory until it is dropped or the CAS server restarts. To keep the data: Set CAS_PERSIST_ON_SHUTDOWN=true to save the table to the caslib's data source as <table>.<CAS_PERSIST_FORMAT> (Parquet by default) when the pod shuts down gracefully. This doesn't run if the pod crashes or is killed with SIGKILL. Or schedule a separate Viya job that calls table.save regularly. This is the more robust option for production. When the consumer restarts and finds the table already in CAS, it appends to it. It doesn't reload the persisted file. If CAS has restarted in the meantime, load the saved file back into memory (and promote it) before you restart the consumer. Otherwise the consumer creates a new table from the next batch, and with CAS_PERSIST_ON_SHUTDOWN=true the next shutdown overwrites the saved file with that new, smaller table. Session-scoped tables With CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE=false, the table belongs to the consumer's CAS session. Other users can't see it, and it disappears when the pod restarts. Use this only for testing.

upload_frame infers CAS column types from the first batch, and every later batch is appended to that schema. This means: A new field in later messages, or a different type for an existing field (for example, a number that becomes a string), can make the append fail. The batch is retried and then the pod exits with code 1. Because the offset isn't committed, the pod crash-loops on the same batch. Fields that are missing from some messages become missing values. Fields that are missing from every message in the first batch don't exist in the table at all. Ways to handle schema changes: Keep message schemas stable, or version them onto separate topics and tables. After an intentional schema change, drop (or rename) the target table and restart the consumer so it creates a new one. Pre-create the target table in CAS with explicit column types. The consumer appends to an existing table instead of creating one.

Delivery is at-least-once (see Delivery guarantees). Rows can be duplicated when a pod stops between a CAS write and the offset commit, or when a retried write partly succeeded. Deduplicate on _kafka_topic, _kafka_partition, _kafka_offset, for example with a periodic deduplication.deduplicate action or in downstream data preparation.

Every log line is JSON on stdout, so you can ship the logs to any log aggregator and alert on them. Useful signals: Log message Level What it means Batch processed INFO One line per batch, with received, written and parse_failures. Use it to track throughput and parse-error rate Batch appended to CAS / Initial CAS table created INFO Per-batch CAS write details (rows, table, caslib) Skipping unparseable message WARNING A message wasn't valid for MESSAGE_FORMAT. Includes topic, partition, offset and the error Fatal error in stream runner ERROR The process is about to exit with code 1. Includes the stack trace You can track consumer lag with your usual Kafka tooling, for example kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group <KAFKA_GROUP_ID>. Liveness probe The liveness probe in k8s/deployment.yaml only checks that the Python interpreter can start inside the container. It doesn't detect a stalled consumer. Fatal errors make the process exit, which Kubernetes does notice, but you should still alert on consumer lag or on Batch processed lines stopping.

Symptom Likely cause and fix Pod exits right away with Configuration error: Required environment variable X is not set (exit code 2) A required variable is missing from the ConfigMap. Required: KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, KAFKA_TOPIC, KAFKA_GROUP_ID, CAS_HOST Cannot dlopen [tkmk.so] : [libnuma.so.1 ...] on startup The image is missing libnuma1. Build from the provided Dockerfile, or install libnuma1 and libgomp1 in your own base image Pod fails to start with a FileNotFoundError for /etc/.../token or similar A *_FILE variable points at a file that isn't mounted. Check that the Secret exists and has the expected keys Kafka authentication or TLS errors Check the SASL mechanism, the credentials, and that KAFKA_SSL_CA_LOCATION contains the CA that signed the broker certificates. Check the NetworkPolicy ports (9093 by default) CAS connection fails with a TLS error CAS_SSL_CA_LIST must point to a bundle that contains the Viya CA CAS connection fails with 401 / authentication errors The OAuth token has probably expired. Refresh the Secret and restart the Deployment (see Rotation) CAS append failed and the pod crash-loops The message schema no longer matches the table. See Schema changes Consumer is running, but no Batch processed lines appear No new messages. With KAFKA_AUTO_OFFSET_RESET=latest, a new consumer group only sees messages produced after it joined. Use earliest (or a new group ID) to read existing messages The table isn't visible in SAS Studio or Visual Analytics Use CAS_TABLE_PROMOTE=true, and check that the viewing user has read access to the caslib Consumer is evicted from the group or rebalances repeatedly A CAS write (including retries) took longer than KAFKA_MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS. Reduce BATCH_SIZE, or increase the interval

The producer/ package is a Kafka producer that generates a realistic stream of card-payment transactions for end-to-end testing. It's modeled on a fraud-detection use case: a fixed population of cards and accounts, mostly legitimate traffic, configurable bursts of known fraud patterns, geo-aware merchants, MCCs, and several payment channels. The producer ships in the same container image and uses the same Kafka authentication setup as the consumer. Only the entrypoint is different: python -m producer.main.

Every record is a JSON object. Messages are keyed by account_id, so all transactions for one card land on the same partition and stay in order. { "transaction_id": "txn_8d9c7b6a5e4f3210", "event_time": "2026-05-27T10:42:13.812Z", "account_id": "acct_00004217", "card_id": "5499207421896013", "card_bin": "549920", "merchant_id": "mer_000241", "merchant_name": "REWE Supermarket", "merchant_mcc": "5411", "merchant_country": "DE", "merchant_city": "Berlin", "amount": 38.71, "currency": "EUR", "channel": "contactless", "device_id": null, "ip_address": null, "lat": 52.521, "lon": 13.404, "is_fraud": false, "fraud_pattern": null } card_id passes the Luhn check but is entirely synthetic. channel is one of chip, contactless, magstripe, online, atm. device_id and ip_address are only filled in when channel is online. is_fraud and fraud_pattern are ground-truth labels. You can train models against them or use them to check end-to-end correctness. Once the consumer writes these records to CAS, each row also gets the Kafka lineage columns described in Architecture.

On each emission, a fraud burst starts with probability PRODUCER_FRAUD_RATE. The generator picks one of five patterns and emits all of that burst's messages back to back: Pattern Shape Typical detection signal velocity 6–12 small online charges on one card within about 30 s N transactions in T seconds on the same card geo_jump A domestic transaction, followed minutes later by one in a high-risk foreign country Geo-impossibility check high_amount One charge of 25–80× the account's typical amount Z-score on the amount distribution card_testing 4–9 micro-charges across different merchants Amount + merchant entropy cnp_foreign A single online transaction from a high-risk country Channel + country score These patterns are deliberately easy to detect. The point is to validate the pipeline (Kafka → CAS), not a model.

kubectl apply -f k8s/producer-job.yaml kubectl -n swat-streaming logs -f job/swat-streaming-producer By default the Job sends 50 messages/s for 10 minutes with a 2% fraud rate and seed 42. To change those values, edit the env: block in k8s/producer-job.yaml. The Job uses restartPolicy: Never and backoffLimit: 0, so a configuration error fails fast instead of retrying. Finished Jobs are cleaned up after 10 minutes (ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600). Credentials The example Job reuses the consumer's kafka-credentials Secret, which only works if that principal can write to the topic. In real environments, keep the consumer read-only and give the producer its own principal and Secret. See Producer credentials. To re-run the Job, delete it first: kubectl -n swat-streaming delete job swat-streaming-producer.

docker run --rm \ -e KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS=localhost:9092 \ -e KAFKA_TOPIC=viya.events \ -e KAFKA_GROUP_ID=ignored-for-producer \ -e KAFKA_SECURITY_PROTOCOL=PLAINTEXT \ -e PRODUCER_RATE_PER_SECOND=200 \ -e PRODUCER_DURATION_SECONDS=60 \ -e PRODUCER_FRAUD_RATE=0.05 \ -e PRODUCER_SEED=42 \ --network host \ ghcr.io/your-org/swat-streaming:0.1.0 \ python -m producer.main KAFKA_GROUP_ID is required by the shared Kafka configuration, even though the producer doesn't use it. All producer settings are listed in the configuration reference.

The producer logs a progress line every PRODUCER_FLUSH_EVERY messages and a summary at the end: {"level":"INFO","message":"Producer progress","sent":5000,"fraud_sent":412,"elapsed_s":100.1,"actual_rate":49.9} {"level":"INFO","message":"Producer finished","sent":30000,"fraud_sent":2468,"elapsed_s":600.4} fraud_sent counts individual fraudulent messages, not bursts. Because most patterns emit several messages, fraud_sent / sent is noticeably higher than PRODUCER_FRAUD_RATE. If messages aren't arriving, look for Kafka client error lines (authentication failures, unknown topic, TLS problems) and Delivery failed lines. Setting KAFKA_DEBUG=broker,security turns on librdkafka's detailed connection logs.

After the producer finishes, the consumer should have written rows to <CAS_CASLIB>.<CAS_TABLE_NAME>. Some quick checks from a SWAT session: import swat conn = swat.CAS("https://viya.example.com/cas-shared-default-http", username="...", password="...") tbl = conn.CASTable("kafka_stream", caslib="Public") # 1. Row count should match the producer's "sent" (plus any at-least-once replays) tbl.numRows() # 2. Distribution of fraud patterns tbl.groupby("fraud_pattern").summary(subSet=["N"]) # 3. Per-account counts of fraudulent rows; velocity bursts stand out tbl[tbl.is_fraud == True].groupby("account_id").summary(subSet=["N"]) # 4. Geo-jumps: the same account in different countries within minutes tbl[tbl.fraud_pattern == "geo_jump"].head(20) To check for duplicate rows caused by at-least-once replays, list the Kafka positions that occur more than once: conn.loadactionset("fedSql") conn.fedSql.execDirect(query=""" select _kafka_partition, _kafka_offset, count(*) as copies from Public.kafka_stream group by _kafka_partition, _kafka_offset having count(*) > 1 """) If rows with is_fraud = true are present and their count roughly matches the producer's fraud_sent, the pipeline is healthy.

The pipeline downstream of the producer doesn't depend on the message shape, so it's straightforward to swap the generator for another domain. For a trading or order-book use case, for example: order_id, event_time, instrument (AAPL, EUR/USD, BUND), side (BUY/SELL), quantity, price, venue, trader_id, account_id, order_type (LIMIT/MARKET), time_in_force (DAY/IOC/GTC), is_anomaly (spoofing / layering label) Keep the same partitioning approach (key by instrument) and the same burst-injection idea, but replace the fraud patterns with patterns like spoofing (a large quote followed by a cancel) or wash trading (matched buys and sells between related accounts).
